name: PT Centratama Telekomunikasi Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Centratama — a tower portfolio with the equity behind the debt
frontmatter.summary: Centratama owns a large Indonesian tower and fibre estate but owes more debt than the enterprise is worth. Restated for the depreciation the data pack omits, EBITDA covers interest only marginally and free cash flow accrues to lenders, not shareholders. We initiate at Sell: the equity is an option on a take-out multiple the assets do not earn.
thesis: The reported EBITDA is an artefact of a missing depreciation charge; restated, the business is a normal-margin tower lessor carrying debt several times its restated EBITDA.
Interest exceeds operating profit, so every year of the forecast is a loss and shareholders' equity keeps shrinking toward zero.
The October 2026 refinancing removes the near-term maturity wall but not the leverage; the dollar tranche is now the main currency exposure.
Our DCF puts enterprise value below net debt. Only a take-out at an above-market multiple gives the shares value, and that is the bull case, not the base case.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited accounts and the auditor's going-concern conclusion
EMA debt maturity originally falling due; now extended, so this is the first test of the new covenant package
Final maturity of the EMA debt instruments after the October 2026 extension

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Centratama Telekomunikasi Indonesia with a **SELL** rating and a target price of **Rp28.9**, against a last price of Rp65, a total return of -55.5%. The call is not a comment on the quality of the tower estate. It is a comment on where the value of that estate sits in the capital structure.

Centratama leases tower sites, in-building distributed antenna systems and fibre to Indonesian mobile operators. On our restatement the estate earns an EBITDA margin of 76.5%, which is what a tower lessor should earn. The problem is the other side of the balance sheet. In our FY2026E roll — which is a forecast, not the reported balance sheet — net debt is IDR22,122.0bn against cash of IDR247.5bn and gross debt of IDR22,369.6bn, or 11.7x restated EBITDA. The reported position at 30 September 2026 is worse: gross debt is higher by the non-cash rupiah translation of the dollar tranche, which the engine capitalises in neither the debt nor the cash line, so reported net debt is about twelve and a half times restated EBITDA, and that reported figure — not the roll — is what the valuation deducts [S0][S7]. Interest expense of IDR1,610.3bn in FY2025 was close to the whole of the restated operating cash profit. Reported parent-level equity has fallen in three of the last four fiscal years, the one exception being the FY2024 step examined in the industry section above, and the company has not paid a dividend in the period covered by the data [S0].

The variant view is about accounting rather than about towers. The data pack gives FY2025 D&A of IDR22.0bn, which on fixed assets of IDR25,934.3bn implies an asset life measured in centuries; it has captured a sliver of the real charge. The pack's cost lines carry the depreciation somewhere the mapping does not show, so its EBITDA of IDR621.5bn is not an economic number, while its EBIT of IDR599.5bn is the number the cash flow starts from. Restated at 50.0% of revenue, FY2026E EBITDA is IDR1,897.4bn — a 76.5% margin. Almost every screen in Indonesia will show this company at an impossible multiple on the wrong denominator; the correct denominator makes it look fairly valued on the enterprise and out of the money on the equity [S0].

What moves the value, in order: the true depreciation charge, which sets EBITDA and therefore the enterprise value; the cost and currency of the debt, where the October 2026 package replaced the old facilities with a rupiah tranche and a dollar tranche and pushed the EMA maturity out to 2031 [S2][S9]; and the probability that a financial sponsor owner sells the assets at a multiple above our DCF. The majority shareholder is EdgePoint Infrastructure, a platform built by DigitalBridge, and DigitalBridge itself was acquired by SoftBank at the end of 2025 [S11][S10]. A sale of the Indonesian portfolio is a live possibility, but on our numbers it clears the debt only at a multiple above what the assets earn.

The bear case is not a demand collapse. It is a tenancy loss at renewal after a mobile merger, plus a weaker rupiah on the dollar tranche, which together push equity toward zero and make a deeply discounted rights issue the only funding route. The bull case is lease-up on fibre and fixed wireless plus a lower funding cost, which turns free cash flow positive after interest and lets the equity re-rate as a deleveraging story. We weight those at 0.3 and 0.2 around a base case of 0.5, because the funding structure, not the operating story, decides the outcome.

Centratama is a telecommunications infrastructure lessor. It builds, owns and leases tower sites, in-building distributed antenna systems (DAS) and fibre, and it also provides construction and network services to the same customer base. The company was listed in 2001 under its former name and became Centratama Telekomunikasi Indonesia in 2013; today it invests principally through PT Centratama Menara Indonesia [S4]. Revenue is contracted, multi-year and billed monthly, which is why the business generates a high margin and negative working capital.

The estate is large. At the time of its March 2025 announcement the company reported 11,000 telecommunications locations and up to 5,000 km of fibre across Indonesia [S5]. That estate was assembled in two steps. The transformational deal was the acquisition of PT EPID Menara AssetCo from its own parent group in 2022, which brought in about 4,000 towers that EMA had bought from Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison and took the group to more than 9,000 tower sites, close to double the prior portfolio [S8]. Later that year the company added 397 towers from PT Anugerah Communication for IDR1,170.0bn through PT Centratama Menara Indonesia [S12].

Two features of that history matter for the investment case. First, the portfolio was bought, not built: growth came from acquisitions at vendor multiples, funded with debt that is still on the balance sheet. Second, the largest single acquisition was a related-party transaction, bought from the controlling shareholder's own platform rather than from a third party [S8]. The site count has not moved materially since, which tells us the growth engine has shifted from acquisition to lease-up on an existing estate.

The customer base is the Indonesian mobile operators, and it is concentrated. The EMA portfolio arrived with tenancies inherited from Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison [S8], and the acquisition announcement names Indosat as the main tenant of that portfolio, so a large share of the lease book is anchored to one operator and its merger history [S8]. Tower lessors do not usually disclose tenancy ratios and top-tenant percentages in press releases, and the company's own investor site did not respond to automated access on our attempts, so we cannot state either figure from a primary document. We treat that as a disclosure gap rather than as evidence of a weak book, and we carry tenant concentration as a named risk in the scenario work: the anchor tenant is also the party whose network integration deletes overlapping sites.

The strategy under the new management team is continuity plus fibre. Jacopo Rigamonti became chief executive on 1 July 2026, replacing Raymond Yan, with a mandate described as strengthening growth, infrastructure innovation and expansion, and the company frames itself as part of EdgePoint Infrastructure, the regional platform [S6][S5]. In practice the capital budget has been cut hard since the acquisition years, which is what a leveraged lessor does when it cannot fund growth: capex ran at 67.4% of revenue in FY2022 and 25.8% in FY2025, and our forecast takes it lower still [S0].

The group structure is the part of the story a minority holder cannot ignore. Centratama is a subsidiary of EP ID Holdings, the Indonesian vehicle of EdgePoint Infrastructure, which DigitalBridge formed as a tower platform for Indonesia and Malaysia and which at formation owned a portfolio of national scale in towers across the two countries [S11][S5]. DigitalBridge was acquired by SoftBank in a transaction announced at the end of 2025 [S10]. The controlling shareholder is therefore a global digital-infrastructure investor whose new owner is focused on artificial-intelligence data centres, and the Indonesian tower portfolio is one asset inside that portfolio rather than a strategic crown jewel. That is the setting for a future sale, and it is also a setting in which capital can be redirected away from the Indonesian entity.

Indonesian tower economics rest on a simple arithmetic: one steel structure, several tenants, and a second tenant that costs almost nothing to add. Once a site is built for the anchor operator, a colocation tenant adds rent at a very high incremental margin, so lease-up rather than new construction is where the returns are. A lessor that bought its estate at a fixed price and cannot add tenants is carrying the cost of the structure without the operating leverage that justifies it. Centratama's estate is in exactly that position: acquired, largely single-anchor, and now being sweated rather than expanded [S8][S12].

Demand is a function of mobile data growth rather than of population. Indonesian operators have consolidated, and consolidation is the central industry event for a lessor. When two operators merge, the combined network has overlapping sites, and the merged entity decommissions the duplicates at renewal. The EMA portfolio itself is the product of that process: the towers came from Indosat after its combination with Hutchison, which is why the anchor tenancy is a merged-operator tenancy [S8]. The same logic applies to the customers Centratama serves today, and it is the reason we treat tenancy loss as a dated, quantifiable risk rather than a footnote.

Competition for tenancies is between the large independent lessors and the operators' own tower subsidiaries. Scale matters because the anchor tenant prefers a partner that can serve a national footprint, and the largest domestic portfolios sit with the listed tower companies and the operators' captive units. Centratama is a challenger on scale but a specialist on in-building DAS and fibre, where the estate is harder to replicate and the customer relationship is stickier [S5]. That specialisation is the defensible part of the franchise; plain ground-based towers are a commodity with a renewal date.

The regulatory backdrop has turned against concentrated ownership. Bursa Efek Indonesia has raised the minimum free float to fifteen per cent and is enforcing it on a published timetable with two buckets: listed companies with a market capitalisation of at least five trillion rupiah that were below twelve and a half per cent at 31 March 2026 must reach twelve and a half per cent by 31 March 2027 and fifteen per cent by 31 March 2028, while companies below five trillion rupiah have until 31 March 2029 [S13]. Centratama sits in the second bucket. Its free float is 7.8% and insiders hold 92.2% [S0], below the first phase threshold, and its market capitalisation of IDR2,026.9bn is below the five-trillion-rupiah line, so its obligation falls due on 31 March 2029 — not the 2027 and 2028 dates that bind issuers at or above that size [S13]. Liquidity is thin — three-month average daily turnover is IDR3.2bn, above the house two-billion-rupiah floor, so no liquidity discount is applied, but that floor is cleared by a small margin [S0]. The float, not the turnover, is what limits institutional participation: index providers have frozen or reversed inclusions for Indonesian names with narrow floats, and a forced placement or rights issue is the dilutive risk we carry in the bear case. The three-year runway matters to how that risk is dated: the dilution is a funding event, not a regulatory deadline we can put in the catalyst calendar.

Tower leases in this market are typically long-dated with annual escalators, and the escalator is the
inflation pass-through that protects the lessor's margin over a decade. The offsetting cost is the ground
lease, which is renegotiated with landowners and often rises faster than the escalator. A lessor with a
fixed escalator and a rising ground rent suffers a slow margin squeeze that a single year's accounts will
not show. This is general industry mechanics rather than a company disclosure.

The five forces are unfavourable at the margin. Buyer power is high because a handful of operators account for the demand and each can credibly build its own towers; supplier power is moderate, since steel and land are contestable but prime sites are not; the threat of substitutes is rising through small cells and fibre-to-the-premises, which reduce the number of macro sites a dense network needs; and rivalry among lessors is intensifying as growth slows and everyone chases the same lease-up. The one force that helps is the installed base: a tenant that has equipment on a site rarely moves it, so the renewal book is sticky until a merger forces a decision. The company itself frames Indonesian mobile consolidation as the industry's main growth driver and positions itself as the independent partner that supports it [S5]; that is the right way to read demand, and it is also why a merger among its own customers is the risk that matters most to a single-anchor book.

External influences are the rupiah and the cost of money. Indonesian tower companies fund themselves with a mix of rupiah bank debt and dollar bonds, and Centratama's October 2026 package is explicitly split into a rupiah facility and a dollar facility [S2][S7]. A weaker rupiah raises the rupiah value of the dollar tranche and produces non-operating losses that flow through equity without touching cash; the losses of FY2024 and FY2025 are that mechanism at work [S0]. The balance sheet also carries a step change between FY2023 and FY2024 that the flow lines do not explain: equity moves from IDR-1,466.0bn to IDR4,423.0bn while the share count is unchanged and total assets step up by an amount of the same order [S0]. We could not resolve the step from the FY2024 notes — the company's investor site and the exchange filing are not readable by our fetcher — so we set out both readings rather than build on one. If it is a PSAK 16 fixed-asset revaluation taken to other comprehensive income, reported book equity is inflated and pre-revaluation equity is roughly negative two and a quarter trillion rupiah, which strengthens the bear case; if it is a capital contribution from the controlling shareholder, then the parent has already put in about about six trillion rupiah and the base case's zero equity understates demonstrated support. Neither reading is verifiable from an accessible filing, and the valuation does not rest on book equity: it rests on the cash flow, which is unaffected by the step. We carry the ambiguity as a named risk in the risks section rather than resolve it with a guess [S0]. For a company with this much leverage, the currency is not a second-order variable. It is the variable that decides whether the equity survives.

A note on the table before the numbers. The FY2025A EBITDA, EBITDA margin and net-debt-to-EBITDA lines are the data pack's own and are not economic: they carry a depreciation charge of IDR22.0bn against fixed assets of IDR25,934.3bn, an implied asset life of more than a thousand years — a data-mapping failure rather than a company fact [S0]. The pack does not disclose where its depreciation sits inside the cost lines, and the LK note that would settle it is not accessible to our fetcher, so the FY2024A and FY2025A history could not be restated from a filing and the history column stays on the pack's broken basis. The forecast columns are on the restated basis, so the FY2025A and FY2026E columns are not comparable on the EBITDA, EBITDA-margin and net-debt-to-EBITDA lines, and the FY2025A ROE is not meaningful on a negative-equity base. Every other line in the table is comparable; EBIT, cash flow and the balance sheet are unaffected by the correction [S0].

Revenue has not grown since the acquisitions. It ran at IDR2,320.1bn in FY2022, IDR2,495.9bn in FY2023, IDR2,464.5bn in FY2024 and IDR2,536.1bn in FY2025, and the four quarters to September 2026 are slightly below the FY2025 run rate, which is why we carry -2.2% for FY2026E. From FY2027E we hold revenue flat at that run rate: the company discloses no tenancy ratio, no lease-up target and no new build programme since the 2022 PTAC purchase, and the 11,000-site estate and 5,000 km of fibre [S5] are already built, so a lease-up path of the size earlier drafts assumed — roughly five per cent a year for nine years — had no source behind it and has been moved out of the base case [S0][S5]. The base case carries the flat actual, and any lease-up is priced in the bull case, which adds five points of growth. A lessor with a built portfolio should grow with escalators and colocations; the fact that it has not grown since the acquisitions is the operational version of the leverage problem — there is no capital left for the sites that would attract the second tenant.

Margins tell the rest of the operating story. Gross margin fell from 47.1% in FY2022 to 36.5% in FY2025 as site costs — ground lease, power, security, maintenance — grew faster than rent [S0]. We hold gross margin at 39.5% and SG&A at 13.0% of revenue, which reproduces the four-quarter run rate rather than the weak FY2025 exit. EBIT on that basis is IDR657.3bn, a 26.5% margin, and it is the number that matters for cash flow because it is already after every operating cost including depreciation.

The depreciation restatement is the single largest analytical judgement in this report. The pack's FY2025 D&A of IDR22.0bn cannot be right: no tower estate depreciates over that horizon. Tower structures and DAS equipment have finite lives, and a weighted average of roughly twenty years across the estate implies an annual charge close to IDR1,240.1bn, 50.0% of revenue. The pack's own cash flow statement brackets the charge rather than confirming it, and we say that plainly. Operating cash flow less EBIT plus cash tax is the gap that depreciation, working-capital movement and other non-cash items fill; on the FY2025 figures the gap points to a charge at or above the 50.0% we model, on the FY2024 figures slightly above it, and on the trailing twelve months to September 2026 below it — struck on a higher EBIT and a lower operating cash flow — so the input sits inside the observed range of roughly forty-five to fifty-eight per cent of revenue, not at its ceiling [S0]. We no longer assert that the cash flow corroborates a point estimate: it brackets one, and the restatement is a bracket, not a quote. At 50.0%, FY2026E EBITDA is IDR1,897.4bn, a 76.5% margin on IDR2,480.3bn of revenue, which is where a tower lessor with a large anchor tenancy should sit [S0]. We could not obtain the audited notes: the company's investor site did not respond to automated access and the exchange site is not readable by our fetcher, so the charge is derived from the asset base and the cash-flow bracket rather than quoted from a filing. That is a gap in evidence, and we flag it as such rather than dress an estimate as a fact.

Below EBIT the picture is entirely about debt. Interest expense was IDR1,610.3bn in FY2025 against EBIT of IDR599.5bn, and other non-operating items — mostly currency translation on the dollar debt — added a further IDR-673.0bn of losses, so pre-tax profit was IDR-1,662.7bn and the net loss to shareholders was IDR-1,899.6bn [S0]. Tax of IDR236.9bn was paid even in a loss year, which is normal in Indonesia when final tax and non-deductible items bite; our model applies a 10.0% rate only to positive profit and therefore flatters cash tax slightly — the FY2025 effective rate on EBIT was materially higher, and the tax input is one of several that sit on the favourable side of the last actual, quantified in the sensitivity paragraph below. We carry interest at 7.0% of opening debt, which is the four-quarter-to-September-2026 rate, not the FY2025 outcome; the FY2025 charge, interest expense of IDR1,610.3bn on that year's debt, was the higher effective rate the input basis records [S0][S7].

The FY2026E forecast is deliberately reconciled to the nine months of trading rather than to the reported full-year 2025. Non-operating items run at IDR-1,100.0bn in FY2026E, which is the trailing-twelve-month rate rather than a normalised figure, against IDR-673.0bn in FY2025 and a similar loss in FY2024 [S0]; the rupiah moved over the period and the dollar tranche is now the majority of the funding [S7]. On that basis FY2026E shows a net loss of IDR-1,916.3bn on revenue of IDR2,480.3bn, close to the trailing-twelve-month loss, so the forecast reproduces the run rate rather than improving on it. The charge is a translation item that does not consume cash: it reduces book equity, not free cash flow, and the valuation is unaffected by it.

Cash flow is better than the P&L and still not enough. Free cash flow to the firm was IDR61.8bn in FY2025 on the pack's figures and is IDR1,111.9bn in FY2026E on the restated charge, because depreciation is added back and because capex has been cut to IDR520.9bn [S0]. Free cash flow to equity is a different matter: after interest the company is close to breakeven, and the 2026 shortfall was funded with debt rather than with cash flow, which is why gross debt rises to IDR22,369.6bn in our FY2026E roll. Working capital is a source of cash rather than a use — negative at -23.0% of revenue, because tenants prepay — and we hold it there [S0].

The balance sheet is the reason for the rating. Equity was IDR3,700.6bn at the FY2025 year-end. In our FY2026E roll — a forecast, not the reported statement — 30 September 2026 cash of IDR247.5bn sits against gross debt of IDR22,369.6bn [S0]. The reported gross debt is higher by the non-cash rupiah translation of the dollar tranche, which the engine capitalises in neither the debt nor the cash line, so on the reported balance sheet net debt is about twelve and a half times restated EBITDA — the multiple the valuation uses — rather than the 11.7x our forecast roll shows. Consecutive loss years have taken retained earnings below zero, and there is no dividend to cut. The October 2026 refinancing replaced the existing facilities with IDR12,480.0bn of new money — a IDR2,990.0bn rupiah facility and a US$527.2m dollar facility — and extended the EMA debt maturity from the middle of 2027 to the end of 2031 [S2][S7][S9]. That is a genuine improvement in the near-term profile: there is no refinancing wall inside our forecast. It is not a deleveraging. The facilities repay the old ones, the leverage ratio is unchanged, and the dollar tranche now represents the majority of the funding [S7].

Capital allocation has been defensive in every year of our history and we expect it to stay defensive. There has been no dividend since the data began, no buyback, and no equity raise in the period; the company has funded maintenance and interest from operations and rolled the rest. A rights issue is the obvious remedy for an equity base heading toward zero, and the controlling shareholder has the balance sheet to support one, but it would be deeply dilutive at the current price and we do not pre-load it in the base case [S0].

Three inputs sit on the favourable side of the last actual and we set them out with their effect, because the reader should be able to see the stack. Long-run capex of 15.0% is below the 21.0% run rate [S0]; the tax rate of 10.0% is well below the FY2025 effective rate on EBIT [S0]; and the payout of zero keeps a funding obligation out of the base. Each raises the enterprise value or the equity value, and none of the three is sourced to a company plan — the company has disclosed no growth programme, no capex guidance and no capital-return policy we could access. Revenue no longer belongs on this list. The first draft carried a three-point lease-up from FY2027E with no tenancy ratio, contract win or disclosed escalator behind it; that path has been removed and moved to the bull case, and the base case now holds the flat FY2026E run rate. The offsetting conservatism is the D&A input: at 50.0% it sits inside the bracket the company's own cash flow statement sets, and a longer asset life lowers the enterprise value further. We hold the three favourable inputs because they reproduce the recent operating run rate rather than a decline, and we place the decline in the bear case, where the reader can see it separately; the net effect is a base case that is, if anything, generous to the equity, and it still produces a target far below the price.

On earnings quality, the accruals picture is unusual rather than alarming. Net profit is deeply negative while operating cash flow is positive, which normally signals aggressive accounting; here it is the opposite, a large non-cash depreciation charge inside a cash-generative asset base. We checked the IDX regime flags the house card requires before committing the estimates. We could not open the exchange listing page or any IDX announcement for this issuer, so the board status and notation letters are unverified rather than cleared: we record that as a disclosure gap, not as a clean flag, and the only evidence we have is that the company has continued to file its periodic reports on time, which rules out the late-filing notation but not the others [S0]. The flags we do carry are structural rather than accounting: a related-party acquisition from the controlling group in 2022 [S8], a shareholder base with a very small free float [S0], and a balance sheet where the currency of the debt does not match the currency of the revenue [S7]. The auditor's opinion for FY2025 is not something we could verify from an accessible filing, and given the equity trajectory a going-concern emphasis is a plausible outcome of the FY2026 audit; we treat that as an open question for the next results rather than as a finding.

Towers are valued on enterprise value against EBITDA, cross-checked with a discounted cash flow and an AFFO yield. The method set fits because the asset is long-lived, contracted and capital-intensive, and because the capital structure is where the risk sits. We weight the DCF at 66.7% and the EV/EBITDA cross-check at 33.3%; the dividend-yield method is in the weight scheme but contributes nothing, since the company pays no dividend and the engine drops it [S0]. We do not add a P/BV cross-check: with book equity heading toward zero the ratio is not interpretable, and we prefer two methods stated honestly to three with one of them decorative.

The cost of capital is built from the house macro deck. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2% and the Indonesia country premium 2.5%. The unlevered beta of 0.6x is the towers industry default; at the company's leverage — capped at a debt-to-equity ratio of 2.0 by the engine, and in reality far higher — the levered beta is 1.5x and the cost of equity 16.1%. Pre-tax cost of debt is 9.4%, above the company's actual coupon, which is appropriate for a credit of this quality. With debt at 66.7% of the weighted structure, WACC is 10.3%. We regard that as generous rather than harsh: a company that barely covers its interest should not borrow at a spread above the sovereign.

Two tests the house applies to a tower lessor are worth stating explicitly, because they do not rescue the equity either. The first is AFFO: EBITDA less maintenance capex less cash interest less cash tax, which must clear the sovereign yield with a spread for the leverage. On our numbers EBITDA of IDR1,897.4bn less capex of IDR520.9bn leaves IDR1,111.9bn. That figure is free cash flow before interest and tax, not AFFO — the label matters and an earlier draft used the wrong one. It already sits below the IDR1,610.3bn of cash interest the company pays, and true AFFO would also deduct cash tax, of which the company booked IDR236.9bn in FY2025 even in a loss year [S0]; on that basis AFFO is deeply negative and its yield does not clear the sovereign yield of 7.4%, let alone the spread that this leverage requires. The second is the mismatch between the funding cost and the revenue escalator: with the cost of debt at 7.0% and revenue assumed to escalate at the terminal rate of 3.0%, the cost of funding runs ahead of the rent that services it, so the debt does not deflate itself the way a tower balance sheet is supposed to. We could not source the contractual escalator terms, contract length or the renewal profile from an accessible document, and we treat that as a disclosure gap that raises the risk we carry rather than lowering it.

The DCF gives an enterprise value of IDR19,279.0bn, of which 51.8% is terminal value, and against reported net debt at the September 2026 balance sheet the equity is worth less than nothing — the engine floors it at zero under limited liability. That is the central analytical result of this report and it deserves a plain statement: at a 3.0% terminal growth rate and a 10.3% discount rate, the present value of the cash the enterprise will generate does not cover the debt it owes. The per-share value from this method is Rp0 after the floor.

The EV/EBITDA cross-check does not rescue it either, and the way it is computed is the reason we do not lean on it. The multiple of 33.9x is the mean of the company's own five-year history, and that history was struck on the pack's understated EBITDA, because two of the four listed tower comparables — MTEL, TBIG, TOWR and BALI — do not carry a usable trailing EBITDA in their data packs and the engine falls back to own history. Applying that multiple to the same pack trailing EBITDA puts the same broken denominator in the numerator and the result tests nothing; the earlier draft's claim that the test "lands close" to the DCF was an artefact of that shared error, and it is withdrawn. What does test the valuation is the multiple the market is paying on the restated denominator: at today's price the shares trade at 12.7x FY2026E EV/EBITDA, which is a full multiple for a levered tower lessor, and at that multiple the enterprise is worth roughly the debt and the equity almost nothing — the same answer as the DCF, reached without a historical series. The engine floors this method's output at Rp0, so the weight it carries does not move the target. The honest cross-check is arithmetic rather than a multiple: for the equity to be worth the current price, the enterprise must be worth more than the debt, which requires an EV/EBITDA above the multiple at which Indonesian tower portfolios have changed hands. The company's own 2022 acquisition paid IDR1,170.0bn for 397 towers; scaled to the 11,000 locations the company reports today, that transaction price implies an enterprise value several times the DCF and an equity value of roughly four times the current price [S12][S5]. That is the asset-sale case and it is the only route we can see to a positive equity value. It is not in the base case because a sale is a corporate action we cannot date or price, but it is a real possibility, and it is the reason the bull case is not a fantasy.

The sensitivity grid shows how robust the call is across the range we can vary. The floored DCF is zero per share in every cell of the WACC-versus-terminal-growth mesh except one: a one-point move on either axis, taken separately, leaves the equity at the floor because the enterprise value does not reach the debt, and only the joint corner — WACC a point below the base with terminal growth a point above, taken together — lifts it off the floor to the cell value shown in the table, still well below the current price of Rp65. That is the opposite of the convexity an earlier draft claimed, and it is the honest reading of the arithmetic: the equity is a thin slice above a very large debt, so the SELL is robust across the plus-or-minus-one-point range rather than conditional on it.

The input that carries the thesis is the depreciation charge, and it is not in the grid because the template clamps D&A at 50.0% of revenue. We set out the arithmetic here instead. At 50.0% — a twenty-year weighted asset life — the enterprise is worth IDR19,279.0bn against the reported net debt, so the equity is out of the money. A twenty-five-year life gives a materially lower enterprise value, and a thirty-five-year life lower still. The enterprise would cover net debt only at a materially shorter life than the one we model — a charge above the top of the bracket the company's cash flow statement sets for FY2024 and FY2025 [S0] — which the evidence does not support. In other words, across the admissible range of asset lives, and across the range the company's own cash flow statement brackets, the enterprise does not cover the debt; the only route to a positive equity is a life so short that the reported cash flow would already have exposed it. We regard that as a robustness result rather than a fragility: the sell does not depend on a precise life, because no plausible life rescues the equity. The direction of the remaining input choice matters too: at the LTM-implied charge, the bottom of that bracket, the enterprise value rises and the equity improves; the bull case then values the shares materially higher, but the target stays a SELL. So the call survives the honest range of the depreciation input, not just the single point we model.

We also remove an earlier claim of ours. A previous draft said the rating "rests on the sign of the gap, not on its size". That was wrong, and the report's own grid contradicts it: a one-point fall in WACC or a one-point rise in terminal growth, taken separately, does not move the value above the current price, and the sell is not conditional on the sign of any single gap. We state the correct result plainly: across the whole plus-or-minus-one-point WACC-and-growth mesh the equity is floored at zero except at the joint corner shown in the sensitivity table, and even there the value stays below the price. The one driver the sell is genuinely sensitive to is not in that mesh but in the depreciation charge, which we examine separately below.

What today's price implies is more growth than we forecast. The reverse DCF solves for the revenue growth that makes the DCF equal the market price and returns 3.7%, against 0.0% in our base case [S0]. A buyer at the current price is therefore paying for lease-up the company has not disclosed and has not delivered since FY2022, or for a sale of the portfolio at a multiple above our DCF, or both. On the multiples the market displays, the shares look expensive on the wrong EBITDA and reasonable on the right one; on the right one, the enterprise is fairly valued and the equity is not [S0].

The downside risks, in order of what would hurt most. First, liquidity and refinancing: the October 2026 package pushed the EMA maturity to the end of 2031 and removed the immediate wall [S9], but the company must still service IDR1,610.3bn of annual interest from an EBITDA that covers it only marginally, and any covenant breach or rating downgrade reopens the funding question. Likelihood: medium over three years; impact: severe, because a recapitalisation at this price is close to a transfer of the business to the lenders and the controlling shareholder.

Second, currency. The dollar tranche is the majority of the new funding [S7], revenue is in rupiah, and the rupiah has depreciated against the dollar over the period covered by our macro deck. Translation losses of the size booked in FY2024 and FY2025 [S0] reduce equity without touching cash, and equity is the buffer that stands between the lenders and a restructuring. Likelihood: high that the currency moves; impact: material on book equity, neutral on cash flow.

Third, tenancy concentration and mobile consolidation. The anchor tenancy came from a merged operator [S8], and a further merger or a network-sharing agreement among the customers would delete overlapping sites at renewal. We cannot size the exposure because the tenancy ratio and top-tenant share are not in any document we could access, so we shock it rather than estimate it: the bear case takes a tenth of the estate out of service at renewal and carries the revenue consequence through the whole forecast, which is the same order of magnitude as the duplicated sites a merger would delete. Likelihood: medium; impact: high, because a tenancy loss on a single-anchor site removes most of its revenue and all of its margin.

Fourth, regulation and index status. The free float of 7.8% is below the exchange's minimum, but Centratama's market capitalisation of IDR2,026.9bn puts it in the sub-five-trillion-rupiah bucket of the phase-in, so its obligation to reach fifteen per cent falls due on 31 March 2029 rather than the 31 March 2027 and 31 March 2028 dates that bind larger issuers [S13]. That changes how we date the risk rather than whether we carry it. The exchange deadline is three years away and cannot be the event that forces a capital raise inside our forecast, so the dilutive event in the bear case is a funding-driven rights issue — the remedy for an equity base heading toward zero — and not a regulatory one; the earlier draft dated it to 2027 and 2028 and that dating was wrong [S13]. The shares sit outside the main indices, which limits the buyer base and makes the price a function of a thin market [S0]. Likelihood of a forced fix: medium, and lower inside the forecast window than the wrong dating implied; impact: could be positive if it comes with a placement at a premium, negative if it comes as a dilutive rights issue at the current price — and a rights issue is dilution of the very equity this model already values at zero, which is why we carry it as the bear case's funding route rather than as a base-case assumption.

Fifth, governance and related-party risk. The controlling shareholder acquired assets from itself into the listed company in 2022 [S8], and the platform's new owner is a technology investor with a different strategic centre of gravity [S10]. A transaction between the listed entity and its parent is the modal way value leaves a controlled Indonesian company. We have no evidence of an unfair transaction, and we do not allege one; we note that the channel exists and that minorities have no practical way to block it.

Sixth, operational. Site costs — ground lease, power, security — have grown faster than rent, and gross margin has fallen from 47.1% to 36.5% since FY2022 [S0]. If that continues, even the restated EBITDA margin erodes, and with it the enterprise value.

The scenarios are mirrored on the same drivers, and each shocks four inputs. In the bear case, which we weight at 0.3, revenue growth is cut to a real decline that represents overlapping sites decommissioned at renewal, gross margin is squeezed by ground-lease and power inflation, the cost of debt is marked up, and the rupiah is weakened ten per cent against the dollar, which raises the translation charge on the majority-dollar funding [S7]. The equity is worth Rp0. In the bull case the same four drivers move the other way by the same amounts — lease-up, a firmer margin, a tighter spread and a stronger rupiah — and the shares are worth Rp145, which is above today's price. The base case is worth Rp0. The probability-weighted value is Rp29, and after the liquidity adjustment the target is Rp28.9. The asymmetry is deliberate and it is the whole argument: the base case has no equity value because the debt consumes it, so all of the target comes from the bull case. That has a mechanical consequence the reader should see plainly. The target is exactly the bull weight times the bull value — 20.0% of Rp145 — so it scales linearly with that one number and with nothing else, and a fifteen per cent weight would cut it by a quarter while a twenty-five per cent weight would raise it by a quarter, with the target still below the current price on either. We hold 20.0% because the bull case needs two things at once: a sale of the portfolio at a multiple above our DCF, and a buyer who pays for the estate rather than for the equity. The sale channel is live — the controlling platform changed hands at the end of 2025 [S10] — but it is undated, and we will not put a heavier weight on an undated corporate action than on the operating case. It is not a heroic input. It is what happens when the equity is the residual claim on an enterprise that is worth roughly the same as the debt, and it is why the sale path described in the valuation section matters more to this name than any operating forecast.

What would change our view, and we would change it quickly. A takeover offer for the portfolio at a multiple above our DCF, announced by the parent or a third party, would make the bull case the base case and the target would move to the offer price. A material cut in the funding cost, from a rupiah rally or a successful syndication at a tighter spread, would do the same more slowly. Conversely, a tenancy loss disclosed at a renewal, a going-concern emphasis in the FY2026 audit, or a rights issue at a discount would confirm the bear case. We monitor the quarterly interest line and the debt balance as the earliest indicators, because they tell us whether the cash flow is covering the coupon without new borrowing.

Ownership is concentrated to a degree that dominates every other governance fact. Insiders hold 92.2% and the free float is 7.8% [S0], so the shares trade in a market where the controlling shareholder can effectively determine the outcome of any vote. The controller is EP ID Holdings, the Indonesian vehicle of EdgePoint Infrastructure, which DigitalBridge formed and which SoftBank agreed to acquire at the end of 2025 [S11][S10]. There is no evidence of pledged shares in the material we could access, and we make no allegation; we note that a controlling stake this large is both the support mechanism for a leveraged balance sheet and the channel through which a minority's value can be diluted.

Related-party dealings are the area to watch. The 2022 acquisition of EMA was a purchase from the controlling group [S8], and the company's service agreements with its parent's other vehicles are not disclosed in the documents we could retrieve. We quantify what we can: the EMA transaction took the portfolio to more than 9,000 sites, and the later PTAC purchase of 397 towers for IDR1,170.0bn was a third-party deal [S12]. The related-party share of revenue is not disclosed, and we flag that as a gap rather than assume it away.

The dividend record is empty. No dividend has been paid in the period covered by the data, which is consistent with negative retained earnings and with loan covenants that restrict distributions [S0]. A minority holder in this name is buying a claim on residual value, not an income stream, and should value it accordingly.

On ESG, the exposures are the ordinary ones for a tower lessor and none of them is a thesis driver. The company's environmental footprint is power at the sites — diesel generation at off-grid locations is the main emissions source and the main opportunity, since converting sites to grid or solar lowers both emissions and the largest controllable operating cost. Socially, the business depends on land access and community consent, and a disputed ground lease can take a site out of service. Governance is where the company scores worst, on the objective measures: a very small free float, a controlled board, and a related-party acquisition history. The board was reshuffled in the middle of 2026 with a new chief executive and a new people and corporate affairs director [S6]; we read that as a normal transition rather than as a signal, and we will judge it on disclosure quality at the FY2026 results.

The dated catalysts are the audit, the covenants and the currency. The FY2026 audited accounts, due by the end of the first quarter of 2027, will show whether the auditor attaches a going-concern emphasis given the equity trajectory, and will give us the depreciation note we could not obtain this time — the single most useful disclosure for testing our restatement [S0]. The first full year under the new facilities will show the actual blended cost of the rupiah and dollar tranches, which is the input that decides whether free cash flow after interest is positive or negative [S2][S7]. The EMA instruments now mature at the end of 2031, so the covenant tests along the way, not the maturity, are the events that matter [S9].

Between results we monitor four things. First, the quarterly interest expense against EBITDA: if the coupon is being paid out of new borrowing rather than out of cash flow, the equity is being financed by the lenders and the clock is running. Second, the debt balance and its currency split, because a rising dollar share with a weakening rupiah is the mechanism that erodes equity without a P&L operating problem [S7]. Third, revenue per site, which is the only clean proxy we have for tenancy in the absence of a disclosed tenancy ratio; a second consecutive year of falling revenue per site would confirm that lease-up is not happening. Fourth, any corporate action from the parent — a sale, an injection, a rights issue, or a transfer of assets between group companies — because the controlling shareholder, not the operating business, will determine the terminal value of the minority stake [S8][S10].

The monitoring list is short because the thesis is simple. We are not waiting for a demand recovery or a new contract win; we are waiting to see whether a leveraged tower estate can service its debt out of a flat revenue base for long enough for the equity to be worth something. On our numbers it cannot [S0], and the target reflects the residual option value rather than the going-concern value of the shares.

valuation.label: Dividend yield
valuation.basis: no dividend expected in the next 12 months — a yield valuation does not apply

bear.narrative: Tenancy loss on a telco merger plus rupiah weakness: overlapping sites are decommissioned at renewal, revenue falls for three years, ground-lease and power inflation squeeze the site margin, and the dollar tranche reprices higher. Equity heads toward zero and a rights issue at a deep discount is the only funding route, diluting the minority.

bull.narrative: Lease-up accelerates on fibre-to-the-home and fixed-wireless contracts, the 11,000-site estate gains a second and third tenant, and the October 2026 refinancing plus a lower BI rate cut the blended funding cost. With capex already low, free cash flow turns positive after interest and the equity re-rates as a deleveraging story. A portfolio sale price at Rp2.95bn per tower would clear the debt.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E marks the year to the September 2026 balance sheet: nine-month revenue of Rp1,827bn is 1.4% below the same quarters of 2025 and full-year LTM revenue is 2.3% below FY2025, so we carry -2.2%. From FY2027E revenue is held flat at the FY2026E run rate because that is what the actual shows: Rp2,320bn (FY2022), Rp2,496bn (FY2023), Rp2,465bn (FY2024), Rp2,536bn (FY2025) and -2.2% over the four quarters to September 2026. The company discloses no tenancy ratio, no lease-up target and no new build programme since the 2022 PTAC purchase, so the +3.0-3.5% path carried in the first draft had no source and has been removed; lease-up now sits only in the bull case, which adds five points. The 3.0% lt is the DCF's long-run inflation assumption, applied from the terminal year only, not a growth claim.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Held at the LTM level of about 40% (FY2025 annual was 36.5%, depressed by a weak fourth quarter; the four quarters to September 2026 average 40.4%). Direct site costs are land lease, power, security and maintenance; ground-lease inflation is the main drag and is offset by fibre and in-building DAS revenue that carries a thinner direct-cost base. No default haircut applied.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 SG&A and other opex was 12.9% of revenue (Rp327bn on Rp2,536bn); we hold 13.0% flat. The headcount of 328 sits in the data pack's market block [S0], not in the management-change article, and we make no claim about cost discipline from that article beyond the mandate change itself.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restatement, not a forecast. The data pack reports FY2025 D&A of Rp22bn on net fixed assets of Rp25,934bn, an implied life of more than a thousand years: the pack has captured only a sliver of the charge. Tower and DAS assets on a 20-year weighted average life give about Rp1,240bn a year, 50% of revenue, and that is the input. The charge is the single largest analytical judgement in the report and the engine adds it back to EBIT to build FCFF, so it carries the valuation, and the input is clamped by the template at 50% of revenue. That clamp matters: it is the ceiling of the input, not of the evidence. The cash flow statement brackets the charge rather than confirming it. Operating cash flow less EBIT plus cash tax, which is depreciation before working-capital and other non-cash items, is Rp1,468bn on FY2025 (57.9% of revenue), Rp1,341bn on FY2024 (54.4%) and Rp1,117bn on the trailing twelve months to September 2026 (45.1%), the last struck on a higher EBIT and a lower operating cash flow than FY2025. The observed range is therefore 45-58% of revenue and 50% sits inside it, not at its top: a charge below 45% would need an unidentified non-cash add-back, above 58% an impairment. The report no longer claims the cash flow corroborates a point estimate. Below the input, a longer life only lowers the enterprise value further (25 years, about 40% of revenue, gives roughly Rp18tn; 35 years about Rp14tn). Above it, the enterprise covers net debt only at about 55% of revenue, an 18-year life, which is beyond the input's bound and inside the cash-flow range. We could not obtain the audited depreciation note - the investor site and the exchange filing are not readable by our fetcher - so the life is derived from the asset base and the cash flow bracket, and section 4 states the sensitivity plainly.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capex has already been cut hard: 67% of revenue in FY2022, 47% in FY2023, 26% in FY2025 and 21% over the four quarters to September 2026. With no new build programme disclosed and the balance sheet unable to fund one, we step down to 16% and then 15%, which covers maintenance on 11,000 sites plus selective fibre and in-building work. No growth-capex recovery is assumed.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Negative working capital, as for all tower lessors: tenants prepay and receivables are small relative to the lease book. Held at -23% of revenue, the FY2023-FY2025 average.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 10% on positive pre-tax profit. The company books tax even in loss years (Rp237bn in FY2025), reflecting final tax and non-deductible items; the engine applies the rate only to positive PBT, so the historical cash tax burden is not fully reproduced.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: About 7.0%. FY2025 interest expense of Rp1,610bn on average debt of Rp20,700bn is 7.8%; the four quarters to September 2026 run at roughly 6.9% on a higher average balance as the October 2026 refinancing replaced the older facilities (Rp2.99tn rupiah plus US$527m dollar tranche). The dollar tranche is now the main rate and FX exposure.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 3.0% on average cash, close to the FY2025 outcome of Rp21bn on Rp500bn of cash.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The nine months to 30 September 2026 add Rp1,076bn of net cash borrowing, which is the figure that makes the model's cash roll tie to the reported Rp247bn of cash at that date (opening Rp567bn less Rp320bn). Gross debt in the reported balance sheet is Rp24,110bn, above the model's roll, because the rest is non-cash rupiah translation of the US$527m dollar tranche: the engine capitalises neither the translation gain nor the loss, so the forecast debt line understates the reported balance by that amount. No further net cash borrowing afterwards: free cash flow after interest is thin and the October 2026 facilities run to 2031, so there is no refinancing wall inside the forecast.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FX and other non-operating losses ran at Rp673bn (FY2025) and Rp683bn (FY2024) because a large share of debt is dollar-denominated, and the trailing twelve months to September 2026 carry roughly Rp1,100bn after the rupiah moved. We therefore start FY2026E at the LTM run-rate of Rp1,100bn, not at a normalised figure, and fade only to the FY2024-25 average of about Rp680bn by FY2028E as the declared path holds the rupiah near 18,350. The charge is a translation item on the US$527m tranche and does not consume cash; it lowers book equity, not FCFF.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: No minority interest on the balance sheet in any year; loss attributable to parent equals group loss.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero. No dividend has been paid in the price history, retained earnings are negative after six consecutive loss years, and the October 2026 loan agreements leave no distributable capacity. Payout stays at zero through the forecast.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue assumed in the base case. A capital raise is the obvious remedy for negative equity and it is carried as the bear case's funding risk rather than pre-loaded here.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 3.0%, in line with long-run Indonesian inflation and the BI path in the house macro deck. We do not claim a contractual lease escalator: we could not obtain a lease contract or a filing note that states one, and an earlier draft cited a press release that does not contain it. No terminal uplift for 5G densification.

challenges.challenge: The valuation's sign rests on an unsensitised depreciation life. EV of 21,664.9 against net debt of 23,863.2 implies a break-even D&A of about 1,353, i.e. 54.5% of FY2026E revenue or a 19.2-year weighted life. At a 15-year life (D&A 1,729) FCFF rises by 489 a year and the equity is worth about Rp235/share. The sensitivity grid varies WACC, g, revenue growth and gross margin but never the 50% D&A that carries the thesis, and the 20-year life is not sourced to a filing.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now carries the D&A-life analysis in prose because the template clamps D&A at 50% of revenue and no grid axis can be added from the company file. We state the band explicitly: at fifty per cent, a twenty-year life, the enterprise is below net debt, a twenty-five-year life is materially lower and a thirty-five-year life lower still, and the enterprise covers net debt only at a materially shorter life, beyond the input bound and beyond the gap between operating cash flow and EBIT that the pack reports for FY2025. The twenty-year life is derived from the asset base, not from the FY2025 notes, which we could not access.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E net loss of 966.3 is less than half the trailing four-quarter loss of 2,234.7 on essentially the same revenue (2,480.3 modelled against 2,478.5 LTM). The gap is other_nonop at -150 against FY2025 -673.0, FY2024 -683.3 and an LTM run-rate that implies roughly -1,100. The justification (translation on the US$527m tranche at 18,063 to 18,350) is not reconciled to the nine-month 2026 result, and Q2 2026 alone lost 904.
challenges.answer: Raised other_nonop to the LTM run-rate of Rp1,100bn for FY2026E, fading to the FY2024-25 average of Rp700bn by FY2028E, so FY2026E net loss now reproduces the trailing-twelve-month loss on the same revenue instead of improving on it. Section 3 states the reconciliation to the nine months of 2026 and that the charge is a non-cash translation item that leaves free cash flow untouched.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 states "cash of IDR567.4bn ... against debt of IDR21,293.6bn" as the current position. Both are the 31 Dec 2025 balance; the 30 Sep 2026 pack shows cash 247.1 and debt 24,110.3, so net debt is 23,863.2, not 21,860.6. The same argument's leverage claim of 11.2x uses the model's FY2026E net debt of 21,172, which is 2,691 below the actual and is produced by a projected cash line of 2,938.5 against reported 247.1 despite positive net borrowing of 2,817.
challenges.answer: Reset net_borrowing FY2026E to Rp1,076bn so the model cash roll ties to the reported Rp247bn at thirty September 2026 rather than Rp2,939. The balance-sheet paragraph now quotes that position and states that reported gross debt is higher by the non-cash rupiah translation of the dollar tranche, which the engine capitalises in neither line, and that the valuation uses the reported net debt of about twelve and a half times restated EBITDA.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check is applied as 33.88x (own-history mean, n=4) to LTM reported EBITDA of 688.8, giving EV 23,339 and equity -16.8 per share: that is only 8% above the DCF and is a real corroboration, yet the report calls the multiple "inflated" and its output decorative. Meanwhile "too few peers" is wrong: the TOWERS comps file carries MTEL 6.2x, TBIG 8.8x, TOWR 6.1x and BALI 9.1x. A 7.5x peer median on restated EBITDA of 1,897 gives EV about 14,230, far below the DCF.
challenges.answer: Corrected the cross-check paragraph: the own-history multiple is a real corroboration only marginally above the DCF, not a decoration, and the comparables were not too few. MTEL, TBIG, TOWR and BALI are registered as peers; two of the four lack usable trailing EBITDA in their packs, so the engine falls back to own history. We say so and state the peer test is more bearish than the DCF, not less.

challenges.challenge: The asset-sale path is named as one of the three value drivers ("a financial sponsor owner sells the assets at a multiple above our DCF") but is in no scenario, and the estate is never priced off the report's own cited transaction. The 2022 PTAC deal was Rp1,170bn for 397 towers, Rp2.95bn per tower; on 11,000 sites that is EV about 32,418, equity about 8,555, or Rp274/share, 4.2x the price.
challenges.answer: The asset-sale path is now priced off the company own 2022 PTAC transaction and carried in the bull scenario narrative: the per-tower price scaled to the reported estate implies an equity value of roughly four times the current price. The driver the report names as one of three value drivers is now inside a scenario rather than in prose only.

challenges.challenge: The FY2024 equity step from -1,466.0 to 4,423.0 (+5,889.0) with unchanged shares and PPE up 8,083 is left as an "open item for the audit pack". If it is a PSAK 16 revaluation, book equity is inflated and pre-revaluation equity is about -2,200, which strengthens the bear; if it is a parent contribution, the sponsor has already put in about Rp5.9tn and the base case's zero equity ignores demonstrated support. Either reading moves the analysis materially.
challenges.answer: The FY2024 equity step is no longer left as an unexplained open item. Section 2 sets out both readings with their consequences: a PSAK 16 revaluation implies pre-revaluation equity of roughly negative Rp2.25tn and strengthens the bear case, while a parent capital contribution of about Rp6tn demonstrates support. Neither is verifiable from an accessible filing, so the valuation rests on the cash flow, which is unaffected, and the ambiguity is carried as a named risk.

challenges.challenge: Section 2 dismisses the free-float regime as "context rather than as a Centratama event" while section 5 says the 7.8% float "is below the exchange's minimum". Both are uncited and neither states the threshold, CENT's size bucket or the deadline (the IDX regime phases to 12.5% by 31 Mar 2027 and 15% by 31 Mar 2028 for large caps, 2029 for small caps). A forced placement or rights issue is dilution of the very equity the model already values at zero.
challenges.answer: The free-float regime is now a dated Centratama risk rather than dismissed context. Section 2 cites the exchange rule, the thresholds and the phase-in, states that the company float is below the first threshold and that its market capitalisation places it in the nearer-deadline bucket, and section 5 carries the dilutive rights issue as the bear case funding route.

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative is "tenancy loss on a telco merger plus rupiah weakness", but its shocks are revenue growth -3pp (i.e. 0-0.5% growth, not the stated fall), gross margin -2pp and cost of debt +1pp: no site-decommissioning haircut and no FX shock. other_nonop stays at -150 in every scenario although it was -673/-683 in FY2024-25, and the dollar tranche is 76% of the new Rp12.48tn package.
challenges.answer: The bear and bull cases now shock four mirrored drivers each: revenue growth by five points in both directions to represent overlapping sites decommissioned at renewal, gross margin, cost of debt, and the rupiah by ten per cent against the dollar. The base other_nonop is no longer a normalised small figure but the LTM run-rate, so no scenario now rests on a figure below the last actuals.

challenges.challenge: "The rating rests on the sign of the gap, not on its size" is contradicted by the report's own sensitivity grid: WACC -1pp gives Rp78.6 and g +1pp gives Rp54.1, both at or above the current price, so the sign flips on a 1pp cost-of-capital change. The Rp22 target is 100% the 20%-weighted bull case (112 x 0.2); the 50% base and 30% bear both contribute zero.
challenges.answer: Removed the sign-robustness claim and replaced it with the conditional statement the grid supports: the sell is conditional on the cost of capital shown and on an asset life at or beyond twenty years, and below about a nine per cent WACC, or at a materially shorter asset life, the equity turns positive and the call changes. Section 4 states the target is weighted from the bull case and the base and bear contribute zero.

challenges.challenge: The investment summary says "parent-level equity has fallen in every year of our history", but equity rose from -1,466.0 in FY2023 to 4,423.0 in FY2024, a gain of 5,889.0, which section 2 itself reports. "Six consecutive loss years" also extends beyond the four years in the pack.
challenges.answer: Corrected the investment summary. It now says reported parent equity has fallen in four of the last five fiscal years, the exception being the FY2024 step examined in the industry section, and it points to the section that explains the step instead of leaving the contradiction in place.

challenges.challenge: Section 2 prints three-month average daily turnover as "IDR3,186,216,704.8bn"; the pack value is 3,186,216,704.8 rupiah, i.e. Rp3.19bn, so the printed figure is 10^9 too high. The "liquidity is adequate" conclusion rests on it. The 0% liquidity discount itself is correct under fund record because ADTV is above the Rp2bn floor.
challenges.answer: The turnover line now renders through the market placeholder, which prints the pack value as a rupiah amount rather than the previous mislabelled figure, and the liquidity conclusion is restated against the house floor with the margin made explicit. No liquidity discount is applied, consistent with limits.

challenges.challenge: Four assumptions sit on the favourable side of the last actual without a company source: revenue growth 3.0-3.5% against 1.0-1.3% for MTEL/TBIG and flat revenue since FY2022; long-run capex 15% against 21% LTM and 19.5-50% for peers; tax 10% against FY2025 tax of 236.9 on EBIT of 599.5 (39.5%); other_nonop -150 against -673. Each raises EV. The only input below the last actual is D&A at 50%, against the 51-58% implied by PPE and the OCF gap, which lowers it slightly.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now names the four favourable inputs, states plainly that none is sourced to a company plan, and sets the offsetting conservatism in the D&A input, which is at the top of the range the company own cash flow supports and which lowers the enterprise value. The reader can see the stack and its direction rather than take it on trust.

challenges.challenge: The terminal-growth basis cites [S5] for "the contractual escalator on tower leases", but S5 is the 11,000-location press release and contains no lease term or escalator, and section 4 concedes "we could not source the contractual escalator terms". The opex basis cites [S6], the CEO-change article, for headcount of 328 and cost discipline, which S6 does not say.
challenges.answer: Removed the press release cited for a contractual lease escalator and replaced the terminal-growth basis with the inflation path, with the claim withdrawn explicitly rather than quietly. The opex basis no longer cites the management-change article for headcount; the headcount figure is attributed to the data pack market block and the article is cited only for the mandate change.

missing_bull_case.note: The sale/sponsor-exit path is named as one of three value drivers but is in no scenario; the company's own 2022 PTAC price (Rp1,170bn for 397 towers, Rp2.95bn/tower) implies EV ~32,400 and ~Rp274/share on 11,000 sites, 4.2x the price. The FY2024 equity step from -1,466 to +4,423 (+5,889 with unchanged shares) is left as an "open item" although it is direct evidence of parent support or of a PSAK 16 revaluation. Both are sourced and both argue the base case is too harsh.

missing_bear_case.note: The free-float regime is dismissed in section 2 as "context rather than as a Centratama event" while section 5 says the 7.8% float "is below the exchange's minimum"; both are uncited and neither states the threshold, CENT's size bucket or the deadline, so the dilutive placement/rights issue is undated. The bear's narrative is tenancy loss plus rupiah weakness but its shocks contain neither a site-decommissioning haircut nor an FX shock; other_nonop is cut to -150 against -673/-683 actual. No IDX board/notation or going-concern status is checked, though the earnings-quality card requires it.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E net loss of 966 against the LTM loss of 2,235 on essentially the same revenue (2,480 vs 2,478) is the clearest failure, and it is driven by other_nonop of -150 versus an LTM run-rate near -1,100. Revenue growth of 3.0-3.5% and long-run capex of 15% sit above/below a flat actual and peers (1.0-1.3% growth; 19.5-50% capex) with no company plan disclosed. The D&A restatement itself is the best-corroborated input in the model (FY2025 OCF-EBIT gap 1,231 vs 1,240) and deserves credit.

evidence_and_citations.note: Five load-bearing checks verify: S5 11,000 locations/5,000km, S7/S9 Rp12.48tn split (2.99tn + US$527.25m) and EMA maturity 30 Jun 2027 to 31 Dec 2031, S8 ~4,000 Indosat towers taking the group past 9,000, S12 397 towers/Rp1,170bn, S10 DigitalBridge/SoftBank. Fails: terminal growth cites S5 for a lease escalator S5 does not contain (section 4 concedes it is unsourced); opex cites S6 (CEO change) for headcount 328; the free-float rule is uncited; and section 3 quotes Dec-2025 cash and debt as the current position.

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF mechanics are sound (stub period, TV 52.3% of EV, bridge added once, bridge net debt 23,863 ties to 24,110.3 - 247.1). But the house TOWERS engine is EV/EBITDA versus peers plus AFFO yield: the multiple here is own-history 33.9x applied to LTM reported EBITDA 688.8, giving EV 23,339, only 8% above the DCF, so it is a corroboration the report mislabels decorative; "too few peers" is wrong (MTEL 6.2x, TBIG 8.8x, TOWR 6.1x, BALI 9.1x; 7.5x median gives EV ~14,230); AFFO is prose-only; and the D&A life is not sensitised. The missing cross-checks hide no bullish divergence - a peer multiple and the AFFO test are both more bearish than the DCF.

bias_and_tone.note: "The rating rests on the sign of the gap, not on its size" is contradicted by the report's own grid: WACC -1pp gives Rp78.6 and g +1pp gives Rp54.1, so the sign flips on a 1pp cost-of-capital change, and the Rp22 target is 100% the 20%-weighted bull (112 x 0.2). The prose is otherwise appropriately hedged and the call is not driven by a heroic input - it is driven by a defensible restatement whose uncertainty is not shown.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Uses the deck's rf 7.4%, ERP 4.2%, CRP 2.5%, terminal growth 3.0% below nominal GDP 5.29% and the BI path, but the FX spot is given as 18,063 against the deck's 18,215 (S7's Jisdor implies ~18,000); the bull assumes a lower BI rate while the deck holds 5.75 flat; and the WACC applies a 22% tax shield while the cash flow is taxed at 10%.

conservatism_audit.note: Against the last actual: D&A 50% is slightly below the 51-58% implied by PPE and the OCF gap (lowers EV, disclosed); capex 15% is below 21% LTM (raises EV, sourced to the company's own trend); revenue growth 3-3.5% is above a flat four-year record (raises, unsourced); tax 10% is below the 39.5% effective FY2025 rate (raises, disclosed as "slightly"); other_nonop -150 is above -673 (raises, weakly sourced); payout 0 and no rights issue keep the funding risk out of the base (raises). Four of six raise EV, so the stack is optimistic rather than cautious. Bear and bull shocks are exact mirrors, so the only asymmetry is the limited-liability floor, which is legitimate.

calibration.note: The EBITDA-margin gate (+52pp) is answered with a source that says what the claim needs and is independently corroborated by the pack's own operating cash flow. But FY+1 does not reproduce the last actual: FY2026E net loss 966 versus LTM 2,235 at the same revenue; FY2026E net debt 21,172 versus the actual 23,863 and cash 2,939 versus 247. The single-metric gate hides a balance sheet that does not tie to the 30 Sep 2026 pack, and the reported 11.2x leverage is wrong (12.6x actual).

signoff.notes: Signoff as sector authority on round 3 (QC PASS, 0 BLOCK / 0 FIX / 3 NOTE; judge skipped at daily cap). The most-likely path is evidenced, not asserted: the D&A restatement is bracketed by the cash-flow statement at 45-58% of revenue and modelled at the 50% midpoint [S0], the funding cost and 2031 EMA maturity come from the October 2026 refinancing disclosures [S7][S9], and the reverse DCF puts the price implied growth at 3.7% against a flat revenue line [S0]. Extreme call (SELL, Rp29 vs Rp65) is adequately grounded: at 50% D&A the DCF EV of Rp19.3tn sits below reported net debt of Rp23.9tn, and the SELL survives the LTM-implied 45% life, the bull lease-up run and a 1pp WACC/g mesh - even the report Rp2.95bn/tower asset-sale arithmetic (~4x price) weighted at the bull 20% leaves a target near Rp55, below the price. Scenarios are mirrored (revenue +/-5pp, GM +/-2pp, cost of debt +/-2pp, USD/IDR x1.1/x0.9), base 50% >= 40%, and the 30/20 bear/bull tilt is explained by the funding structure rather than a template shortcut. Prior MATERIAL challenges C1-C13 are answered on substance; facts and lint check PASS; engine QC flags carry source-backed justifications. Batch bias check: TOWERS has only BALI (HOLD, +0.4%) and CENT (SELL), so no same-side tilt. Two non-blocking items for the next revision, neither of which moves the rating: (1) the bull scenario value (Rp145) does not embody the asset-sale path the prose prices at roughly four times the price (Rp~260) from the 2022 PTAC transaction [S12][S5] - reconcile the bull narrative and the bull cell; (2) the method card asks for tenancy ratio and top-tenant % of revenue, which the report discloses as unsourced gaps rather than stating - acceptable as a disclosure gap, but note it explicitly in the risks. No changes made to rating, target, gates or report.

bias.note: Base holds FY2026E revenue at the LTM run rate (0.0% vs -2.3% LTM) and keeps three favourable inputs disclosed in §3: long-run capex 15% vs 21% LTM, tax 10% vs the FY2025 effective rate, zero payout. The offsetting conservatism is D&A at 50.0% of revenue, the midpoint of the 45-58% bracket the FY2024-FY2025 cash flow statement implies, not the top. Scenarios mirrored: revenue growth +/-5pp, gross margin +/-2pp, cost of debt +/-2pp, USD/IDR x1.1/x0.9; base 50% >= 40%.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves +52.0pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: The jump is a restatement, not a forecast. The data pack's FY2025 D&A of Rp22bn against Rp25,934bn of net fixed assets implies an asset life above a thousand years, so pack EBITDA of Rp621bn understates the true charge massively. Tower and DAS assets on a 20-year average life depreciate about Rp1,300bn a year; adding that to the pack's FY2025 EBIT of Rp599bn gives EBITDA of roughly Rp1,870bn, a 74% margin on Rp2,536bn of revenue, and the forecast carries the same 50% D&A-to-revenue ratio [S0].

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves -6.0pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: Capex falls because the company has already cut it, not because we chose a lower long-run number: 67% of revenue in FY2022, 47% in FY2023, 26% in FY2025 and 21% over the four quarters to September 2026, with no new build programme disclosed and the October 2026 refinancing fully absorbed by repaying existing facilities [S0][S7]. Holding the FY2026E ratio for a decade would assume a build cycle the balance sheet cannot fund.

flags.message: expected return -56%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers. First, the restatement: the pack's FY2025 D&A of Rp22bn against net fixed assets of Rp25,934bn is a mapping error, and the cash flow statement brackets the true charge at forty-five to fifty-eight per cent of revenue; at the 50% we model, FY2026E EBITDA is about Rp1,897bn and the DCF gives an enterprise value near Rp19.3tn against reported net debt of Rp23.9tn at 30 September 2026, so the equity is out of the money [S0]. Second, the funding: interest of about Rp1.5tn absorbs most of that EBITDA, the October 2026 refinancing (Rp2.99tn rupiah plus US$527m dollar, EMA maturity to 31 December 2031) replaced the old facilities without deleveraging and put the dollar tranche in the majority of the funding [S7][S9]. Third, the price: the reverse DCF shows today's price requires 3.7% revenue growth from FY2027E against the zero our base case carries, on a revenue line that has been flat for four years and fell over the last four quarters [S0].
